title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
hook: Your brain runs two operating systems, and the fast one is usually driving.

slides.heading: Two modes of thinking
slides.body: One mode is quick, automatic, and effortless, like reading a face. The other is slow and effortful, like doing long division. Most daily choices come from the fast one.

slides.heading: Shortcuts that misfire
slides.body: The fast mode leans on mental shortcuts. They save energy but create predictable errors, like judging how likely something is by how easily an example comes to mind.

slides.heading: Losses loom larger
slides.body: With prospect theory, Kahneman and Tversky showed people feel losses more sharply than equal gains, so we often take bad bets just to avoid a sure loss.

slides.heading: Two selves, two stories
slides.body: The self living an experience and the self remembering it disagree. Memory overweights the peak moment and the ending, not how long something lasted.

takeaway: Before a big decision, write down one reason you might be wrong, then deliberately slow down to check it.

title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
author: Robert B. Cialdini
hook: Why you said yes to something you didn't want, and how to notice next time.

slides.heading: Reciprocity
slides.body: People feel pressure to return favors, even small unrequested ones. A free sample isn't only generous. It creates a quiet sense of debt.

slides.heading: Commitment and consistency
slides.body: Once we take a small public stance, we tend to act in line with it. Tiny first agreements can pave the way for much bigger asks later.

slides.heading: Social proof
slides.body: When unsure, we copy what people like us are doing. Reviews, "most popular" badges, and packed restaurants all tap into this.

slides.heading: Authority and scarcity
slides.body: Titles and uniforms make us defer, and things feel more valuable when they're running out. Countdown timers work for a reason.

takeaway: When you feel rushed to say yes, name the tactic out loud ("this is scarcity") and give yourself a day.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
hook: Doing well with money has less to do with smarts and more to do with behavior.

slides.heading: Your history shapes your money
slides.body: People who grew up during high inflation or a crash see risk differently. Nobody's crazy. Everyone is reasoning from their own limited experience.

slides.heading: Time does the heavy lifting
slides.body: Compounding rewards patience more than brilliance. Staying invested for decades usually matters more than finding the highest possible return.

slides.heading: Wealth is what you don't see
slides.body: A fancy car shows spending, not wealth. Real wealth is the money you didn't spend, sitting quietly and giving you options.

slides.heading: Leave room for error
slides.body: Plans break. A cash buffer and modest assumptions let you survive bad luck without being forced to sell at the worst time.

takeaway: Set up an automatic transfer to savings or investments on payday so good behavior happens without willpower.

title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
author: Yuval Noah Harari
hook: How a not-very-special ape ended up running the planet.

slides.heading: Shared stories
slides.body: Harari argues humans took over because we can cooperate in huge groups around things that exist only in our heads, like nations, laws, and money.

slides.heading: Farming's mixed deal
slides.body: Agriculture let populations boom, but Harari suggests many early farmers worked harder and ate a narrower diet than foragers did.

slides.heading: Forces that unify
slides.body: Money, empires, and universal religions pulled scattered cultures into larger networks, making strangers able to trust and trade with each other.

slides.heading: Admitting ignorance
slides.body: The scientific revolution took off when people accepted they didn't know everything, and began investing in research to find out.

takeaway: Pick one thing you treat as "just how it is" (a job title, a currency) and ask what shared belief keeps it working.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
hook: Tiny changes, repeated daily, quietly compound into big results.

slides.heading: Systems beat goals
slides.body: Winners and losers often share the same goals. What differs is the daily process. Focus on the system and the results tend to follow.

slides.heading: Change your identity
slides.body: Instead of "I want to run a marathon," think "I'm a runner." Each small action is a vote for the kind of person you're becoming.

slides.heading: Four levers
slides.body: Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. Flip each one to break a bad habit: invisible, unattractive, hard, unsatisfying.

slides.heading: Design your space
slides.body: Environment often beats motivation. Put the guitar in the middle of the room and the phone charger outside the bedroom.

takeaway: Shrink a habit you keep skipping into a two-minute version, like one push-up or one page, and do it today.

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
hook: In a world of pings, the ability to focus for hours is a career superpower.

slides.heading: Focus is rare and valuable
slides.body: Work that needs sustained concentration, like writing, coding, or strategy, is where most real value gets made, and it's getting harder to do.

slides.heading: Switching leaves residue
slides.body: After you check a message, part of your attention stays stuck on it. Constant quick checks mean you rarely think at full strength.

slides.heading: Schedule depth on purpose
slides.body: Block regular, distraction-free sessions with a set place, time, and goal. Treat them like meetings you can't cancel.

slides.heading: Train your attention
slides.body: Resist reaching for your phone at every idle moment. Getting comfortable with boredom makes it easier to stay with hard problems.

takeaway: Book one 90-minute block tomorrow with notifications off, and decide now exactly what you'll work on.

title: Why We Sleep
author: Matthew Walker
hook: Sleep isn't downtime. It's when your brain and body do some of their most important work.

slides.heading: Two sleep signals
slides.body: Sleepiness builds from a chemical called adenosine the longer you're awake, while your internal body clock separately sets when you feel alert or tired.

slides.heading: Caffeine borrows energy
slides.body: Caffeine blocks adenosine's signal instead of removing it. When it wears off, the built-up sleep pressure is still waiting for you.

slides.heading: Memory needs sleep
slides.body: Sleep helps lock in what you learned during the day. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam works against the very thing you're trying to do.

slides.heading: Protect the basics
slides.body: A consistent schedule, a cool and dark room, and less alcohol near bedtime all help. Alcohol can knock you out but fragments sleep.

takeaway: Pick a wake-up time and keep it every day this week, weekends included.

title: Pale Blue Dot
author: Carl Sagan
hook: One tiny pixel photographed from deep space changes how you see everything.

slides.heading: The photo
slides.body: In 1990, Voyager 1 looked back from beyond Neptune's orbit and captured Earth as a speck smaller than a pixel, caught in a sunbeam.

slides.heading: Humbling upgrades
slides.body: Science has repeatedly moved us away from the center: Earth orbits the Sun, which is one star among billions. Sagan saw this as clarifying, not crushing.

slides.heading: A tour of worlds
slides.body: Sagan walks through what robotic missions revealed about other planets, and what their strange climates teach us about our own.

slides.heading: Why explore
slides.body: He argues that learning to travel beyond Earth is both a natural human urge and a long-term way to protect our species.

takeaway: Look up the Pale Blue Dot image tonight, then spend five minutes asking what actually matters in your week.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
author: Clayton M. Christensen
hook: Why great companies can do everything right and still get wiped out.

slides.heading: Good management, bad outcome
slides.body: Leading firms listen to their best customers and chase higher margins. That sensible behavior is exactly what blinds them to certain threats.

slides.heading: Sustaining vs. disruptive
slides.body: Sustaining innovations improve products for existing customers. Disruptive ones start out worse on those measures but are cheaper, simpler, or more convenient.

slides.heading: Starting at the bottom
slides.body: Disruptors often win low-end or brand-new customers that incumbents ignore, then improve until they're good enough for the mainstream.

slides.heading: How to respond
slides.body: Christensen suggests giving a disruptive project its own small, independent unit whose customers and cost structure fit the new market.

takeaway: List one cheaper, "not good enough" competitor in your field and ask what happens if it keeps improving for five years.

title: The Selfish Gene
author: Richard Dawkins
hook: Evolution makes more sense when you look at it from the gene's point of view.

slides.heading: Genes are the replicators
slides.body: Dawkins argues natural selection is best understood at the level of genes, which copy themselves across generations while bodies come and go.

slides.heading: Bodies as vehicles
slides.body: Organisms are, in this view, the machines genes build to get themselves copied. The "selfish" label is a metaphor, not a claim about motives.

slides.heading: Selfish genes, kind animals
slides.body: Helping relatives or trading favors can spread the genes behind that behavior, which explains how real cooperation evolves.

slides.heading: The birth of the meme
slides.body: Dawkins coined "meme" for ideas and habits that spread from mind to mind, copying and mutating a bit like genes do.

takeaway: Next time a trend spreads online, ask what makes it easy to copy. That's the meme idea in action.
